Legal formalism is both a descriptive theory of how judges decide cases and a normative theory of how judges should decide cases . [ 1 ] In its descriptive sense, formalists maintain that judges reach their decisions by applying uncontroversial principles to the facts ; formalists believe that there is an underlying logic to the many legal principles that may be applied in different cases. These principles, they claim, are straightforward and can be readily discovered by anyone with some legal expertise. U.S. Supreme Court Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. , by contrast, believed that "The life of the law has not been logic: it has been experience". [ 2 ] The formalist era is generally viewed as having existed from the 1870s to the 1920s, but some scholars deny that legal formalism ever existed in practice. [ 3 ] [ 4 ]
